articles.title: European shares join a global sell-off as AI spending fears rattle Wall Street and Asian markets
articles.summary: European shares have fallen after sharp losses in Asia and on Wall Street. Doubts over huge AI investments and fears of curbs following the Democrats' US midterm victory have rattled global markets.

image.caption: Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.
Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.
How have European markets reacted?

The pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.
European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks.
Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.
Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.
Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.
Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.
Data centers face backlash from US communities
What's behind the stock rout on Wall Street?
US markets were hammered on Thursday by a sharp retreat in tech stocks, particularly those involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52% and shed as much as $2.5 trillion (roughly €2.23 trillion) in market value, while the broader S&P 500 index plunged 4.4%.
The rout occurred as investors grow increasingly anxious about the colossal AI spending plans and whether they will eventually produce commensurate profits.
The results of the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both houses of US Congress, added to the concerns.

A number of Democratic governors-elect campaigned on slowing artificial intelligence development and promised to stop or pause the construction of data centers amid growing public opposition to such projects.
"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift ​in sentiment," Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo, told the Reuters news agency.

"Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that shows up in the market ​by huge swings in either direction," he said. "That's what we appear to have had — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in."

articles.title: Rodil Zalameda takes oath as 28th Supreme Court Chief Justice
articles.summary: Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda took his oath on Friday as the new Supreme Court Chief Justice, succeeding outgoing Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who retired on the same day.

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 5:21pm
Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda took his oath on Friday as the new Supreme Court Chief Justice, succeeding outgoing Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo, who retired on the same day.
Assuming his post as the 28th Chief Justice of the Philippines, Zalameda took his oath alongside his family before Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen.
Meanwhile, the ceremonial turnover of the gavel was administered by Gesmundo, according to a report by Super Radyo dzBB reporter Christian Maño.
Leonen was one of his four rivals for the position, who also included Associate Justice Benjamin Caguioa, Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao, and Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez.
Malacañang announced Zalameda’s appointment on Thursday, citing his extensive judicial experience across several administrations. Palace said it remains confident in the Judiciary’s impartiality.
It can be recalled that Zalameda penned the SC decision that overturned the graft conviction of former First Lady Imelda Marcos.

He also authored the decision granting a writ of amparo in favor of former Bayan Muna lawmaker Siegfred Deduro, which recognized that red-tagging and guilt by association threaten a person’s right to life, liberty, or security.
Prior to this, Zalameda was appointed as an SC associate justice by then-President Rodrigo Duterte on August 6, 2019.
He also served as an associate justice of the Court of Appeals for 11 years and as the chairperson of its 17th Division.
Zalameda previously served as a branch clerk for the Makati Regional Trial Court.

The new SC chief justice obtained his Bachelor of Laws degree at Ateneo de Manila University in 1987 under an academic scholarship grant. He passed the Bar examinations in 1988. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Ombudsman: 79 flood control-related cases filed in courts
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has filed with Philippine courts 79 criminal cases related to the multi-billion peso flood control corruption scandal, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Friday.

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 5:21pm
The Office of the Ombudsman has filed with Philippine courts 79 criminal cases related to the multi-billion peso flood control corruption scandal, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Friday.
Remulla said that of this number, 75 were filed with the Sandiganbayan while the other four with local courts.

"The ongoing flood control charges include two plunder [cases] which is non-bailable, 22 cases of malversation of public funds, which is also non-bailable because the amount [involved] is above P8.8 million, and 55 violations of Republic Act 3019, the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act," Remulla said in a press conference.

"For flood control, [the amount of projects involved in cases pending] before the court now is P10.78 billion. Remember, there's a much bigger amount involved, but we are working with the evidence that we have so far," Remulla added.
Out of the 79 cases, 67 persons are accused, including the following:

items: 1 senator
1 former senator
4 congressmen
1 former congressman
1 former secretary of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH)
39 DPWH personnel
9 contractors
2 congressional staff
9 private individuals

blocks.text: Further, Remulla said Ombudsman prosecutors have filed 57 non-flood control cases involving 138 respondents.
These 57 cases, Remulla said, involve P13 billion worth of public funds.
The 138 respondents in non-flood control cases include:

items: 78 elected officials
42 DPWH personnel
9 contractors
9 private individuals

blocks.text: "What are the schemes of corruption they are doing? In right-of-way [cases], they fake or falsify land ownership and supporting documents to claim government compensation for right-of-way. These are the ones affected by public infrastructure. Outdated property valuations are also used to inflate compensation claims," Remulla said.

"There are also ghost projects that come out, [the] withdrawing or spending public funds for projects that supposedly do not exist, or releasing funds without the required disbursement vouchers, receipts and other supporting documents," Remulla added. — VDV, GMA News

blocks.caption: From left: Sheara Lupango-Tamaya, SEC Enforcement and Investor Protection Department Director; Rogelio Quevedo, SEC Commissioner; Ren-ren Reyes, G-Xchange Inc. President and CEO; and Atty. Cef Sison, Mynt Chief Regulatory Affairs OfficerThe Securities and Exchange Commission and GCash strengthene…

blocks.text: First formalized in September 2023, the partnership enables close coordination between the SEC Enforcement and Investor Protection Department (SEC-EIPD) and GCash during investigations into online fraud, illegal investment solicitation, unlawful lending, and other offenses.

“Maintaining a secure digital environment and protecting the public from financial crimes requires strong coordination between regulators and digital platforms. Our continued partnership with GCash strengthens the SEC’s capacity to respond promptly and effectively to emerging threats, facilitate the exchange of relevant information, and pursue appropriate enforcement action against individuals and entities that exploit the public through fraudulent and unauthorized investment schemes,” said SEC Commissioner Rogelio Quevedo.

The renewed agreement forms part of the ongoing efforts of GCash to safeguard users from harm by supporting authorities in detecting, investigating, and addressing suspected illegal activities involving the platform.

“Upholding public safety is a commitment we share with the SEC, and this renewed partnership enables GCash to work more closely with regulatory and enforcement agencies when it comes to preventing the misuse of our platform,” said Oscar Enrico Reyes Jr., President and CEO of G-Xchange, Inc. (GXI), the mobile wallet operator of GCash.

As fraudsters attempt to deceive consumers, public vigilance remains an important line of defense against financial cybercrime. Before transacting, the public is urged by the SEC and GCash to verify if prospective investment or lending entities hold valid licenses from official regulatory bodies, such as the SEC or the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). Investment offers promising “guaranteed,” risk-free returns, aggressive recruitment schemes, or loan offers demanding upfront “processing” fees should be treated as immediate red flags.

GCash also reminds users to protect their accounts by never disclosing sensitive credentials, including passwords and MPINs. The superapp emphasizes that it does not send messages containing links, advising customers never to open links sent through SMS, email, or third-party messaging apps.

To stay safe when transacting online, customers are encouraged to report suspicious activities or unauthorized transactions immediately through the GCash Help Center in the app or website, via the Gigi chat support feature, or by calling the GCash hotline at 2882. Scam incidents may also be reported to the Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group by sending an email to acg@pnp.gov.ph.

Partnering closely with regulatory and enforcement agencies, GCash continues to ensure digital financial services remain a safe and trusted channel for all Filipinos. For more information, visit the Help Center.

articles.title: Hidden cameras reveal accessibility barriers at leading restaurants
articles.byline: Jeremy McDonald, Rosa Marchitelli, Jeremy Grimaldi, Daniela Silva

image.caption: Marketplace visited 10 popular restaurant chains with hidden cameras to document the dining experience of customers who have disabilities. (CBC)

blocks.text: Malfunctioning power door operators, inaccessible self-service kiosks and the inability to get a braille menu were among the issues people with disabilities faced while eating out as part of a Marketplace investigation into accessibility at fast-food and full-service restaurants in Ontario.
Marketplace put 10 popular restaurants to the test: five fast-food chains and five full-service restaurants.

The findings raise questions about the effectiveness of Ontario's decades-old accessibility legislation, the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA), and the province's overall approach to fulfilling the act's purpose: achieving accessibility for Ontarians with disabilities.
"There's so much more that can be done," said accessibility strategist Lorene Casiez, who manages Human Space, the accessible design practice of architectural firm BDP Quadrangle.
"There are a lot of better practices, a lot of lived experience … easy-to-do things to make the environment as usable as possible for everyone."
Robert Hampson, who is blind, visited five fast-food chains as part of a Marketplace investigation into restaurant accessibility. (Submitted by Robert Hampson)
Robert Hampson lost his vision at the age of four after undergoing surgery for a brain tumor.

"I remember as a very young kid bumping into things, walking over curbs, hitting my head, but I decided I could do anything I wanted," the Toronto resident said. "I just had to keep going and have no fear."

items: Watch the full investigation, "The Dining Divide," from Marketplace on YouTube, CBC-TV, or CBC Gem on Friday at 8 p.m.

blocks.text: Hampson said his confidence began to wane at a certain point, but it was restored when he decided to take on a mission.
"I need to educate people along the way," he said. "Every time I walk out the front door and step outside, I'm an advocate for people who are blind and people with disabilities."
Testing fast-food restaurants

Hampson, accompanied by a Marketplace producer, visited one Greater Toronto Area location for A&W, McDonald's, Thai Express, Tim Hortons and Wendy's to document his experience as a customer with a disability.
He started each trip with a simple question: Do you have a braille menu?
None of the locations he visited could provide one.
"I would have liked to have at least found one that had a braille menu," he said. "It's something that needs to be improved upon."

Two companies responded directly to the findings regarding braille menus. Tim Hortons said it doesn't offer them because of how frequently its menu changes. Wendy's told Marketplace braille menus are available across the country, but did not explain why Hampson wasn't offered one when he asked.
Accessibility strategist Lorene Casiez says Ontario’s accessibility laws fall short of what's needed for persons with disabilities. (Submitted by Lorene Casiez)
The AODA does not specifically require braille menus, but Casiez said having them on hand sends a positive signal to customers.
"If someone can't visually read, an alternate format might be braille. An alternative format might be an audible component," Casiez said.
"Thinking about different ways that people can understand the information is certainly a requirement in the AODA."
Beyond braille
Marketplace's fast-food restaurant test also included self-service kiosks, layout and washroom accessibility.

Hidden cameras documented Hampson's attempts to use self-service kiosks at McDonald's and Wendy's. Both had touchscreens and some accessibility features, but neither had a way for him to hear options.

At times, Hampson had difficulty navigating. He accidentally went through an emergency exit at Tim Hortons and was heading toward the drive-thru lane when a concerned motorist shouted toward him: "You're in the drive-thru."
Customer who is blind struggles with self-service kiosks
He also got confused on the way to the washrooms at McDonald's and A&W. In the case of A&W, a producer intervened to help him.
On the bathroom door, there was no braille or tactile markings.
"I had no way of knowing, is that the women's? Is that the men's?" he said.
Casiez said a requirement for tactile signage on washroom doors has been in the Ontario Building Code for a long time.
"Not very expensive either, potentially."
Whether the A&W Hampson visited would have been required by the Ontario Building Code to have the signage is unclear.

When it comes to navigating restaurants independently, Hampson wants to see more consistency in how they're laid out. He's also in favour of markings on the ground he can feel with his white cane that can help him determine his location and direction.

items: Why are so many Toronto restaurant toilets in dingy basements?

blocks.text: In a statement, McDonald's Canada told Marketplace it's sorry to hear about the challenges Hampson experienced.
"This restaurant is independently owned and operated, and we have shared the observations provided to us with the franchisee for its review," the company said.

A Wendy's statement said the company is looking into what was documented during the visit and is working with the franchisee to "identify any opportunities to further support the customer experience."

"When this restaurant was built, it was built in accordance with all applicable standards at the time," said a statement from Tim Hortons. "We are working to identify design changes that could in the future better allow all guests to navigate the space independently."
A&W declined to comment on the investigation.
Taylor Lindsay-Noel and a Marketplace producer documented malfunctioning power door operators at chain restaurants in Toronto. (CBC)
Taking on full-service restaurants

Marketplace also visited one location in Toronto for full-service restaurants Boston Pizza, Earls, Milestones, Swiss Chalet and The Keg. At those locations, hidden cameras documented the experiences of two women who use wheelchairs.

Taylor Lindsay-Noel was one of the customers who, along with a Marketplace producer, dined at three of those establishments. She is a social media content creator who does accessibility-focused restaurant reviews.
"I want to show people that we live very full lives, but it also makes it hard for us to live our lives if places aren't accessible," she said.

The checklist included entrances, an area where Lindsay-Noel encountered challenges at Swiss Chalet and Boston Pizza. At Swiss Chalet, the power door operators malfunctioned on the way in and when she left.

items: A lot of restaurants claim to be wheelchair accessible. This reviewer puts it to the test

blocks.text: The same was true of Boston Pizza, but on the way out there was a plant and a sign placed in front of the power door button.
"Even if it was working, I wouldn't have been able to hit it," she said.

Marketplace also documented that there were no power doors at the entrance to The Keg, which is required by the current building code. It's unclear which version of the building code applies to The Keg that Marketplace visited.

The full-service customers also asked employees if they were aware of the AODA, which is supposed to be covered in mandatory accessibility training. Of the five restaurants, only one frontline employee at The Keg said she was "a little bit" familiar with the legislation.
"It's part of who you're serving as your client base. So having an awareness of it is really important," said Casiez.
Government response
Marketplace shared the findings of its investigation with the office of Ontario's minister for seniors and accessibility, Raymond Cho, and requested an interview, but the request was declined.

Instead, his office sent a statement that said: "Individual businesses and organizations are responsible for ensuring they are in compliance with the AODA. The Ontario Building Code also sets out accessibility requirements for new construction and existing buildings undergoing extensive renovations."

A spokesperson for Cho said the ministry focuses its "compliance and enforcement efforts" on areas where it can have the greatest impact and added, "complaint trends are reviewed regularly to help determine which sectors should be prioritized for audits and inspections."
Under the AODA, businesses and non-profit organizations are required to file accessibility compliance reports every three years. The next deadline is Dec. 31.
Full-service restaurants make changes
Marketplace requested interviews with the full-service restaurant chains we documented in our investigation. None agreed to an on-camera interview.

Foodtastic, the parent company of Milestones, said in a statement that Milestones is committed to accessibility and added: "We have taken the opportunity to reiterate to our personnel the importance of being familiar with AODA rules, reminding all employees to ensure their training is up to date."
The company also confirmed it added braille and tactile washroom signs to the location in our test.

A statement from Earls said the location we visited "adheres to all municipal building codes and accessibility requirements." The response also affirmed the company's commitment to "a safe, inclusive and comfortable environment."

Boston Pizza, The Keg and Swiss Chalet provided no response to multiple requests for comment. But since sharing our findings with Swiss Chalet, new power door operators have been installed in the washrooms of the location Marketplace visited.
Swiss Chalet did not respond to Marketplace’s investigation, but has since installed power doors for the washrooms at the test location. (CBC)
Accessibility law 'pathetically weak,' advocate says
The AODA went into force in 2005. The regulations include standards for information and communications, customer service and design of public spaces.
"They're pathetically weak," said Toronto-based disability rights advocate David Lepofsky.
Lepofsky, who is blind, was at the forefront of efforts to create the AODA, but said it hasn't lived up to its potential.
"They deal with the public spaces in the built environment, but virtually nothing about the barriers inside buildings."
Lepofsky is pointing to the fact that many of the requirements for interior spaces are found in the Ontario Building Code, not the AODA. This includes details regarding doors, washrooms and signage.
But, according to Lepofsky, the Ontario Building Code has a crucial flaw: it only applies to new buildings or older buildings that have been extensively renovated.
"For the vast majority of our built environment, the building code's inadequate provisions won't even touch them."
Power doors absent or malfunctioning at popular restaurants
Lepofsky said he wants standards that cover both old and new buildings "comprehensively."
He also wants to see better enforcement of the AODA.
"It's like a voluntary law because people who break the law, even though it has strong financial penalties built into it, sadly don't have to really worry about that at all."
That sentiment was echoed in the 2023 legislative review of the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005, which said "enforcement is non-existent under the AODA."
The review cited a "lack of resources" and "the size of the private sector that falls under the jurisdiction of this legislation."
Restaurants are also subject to Ontario's Human Rights Code, which says every person has the right to equal treatment "with respect to services, goods and facilities."
Disability rights advocate David Lepofsky says Ontario’s accessibility regulations are ‘pathetically weak.’ (Submitted by David Lepofsky)
For Hampson, the restaurant visits were sobering, but he hasn't lost hope.
"It's definitely disappointing and frustrating," he said.

"But I think change comes slowly and it has to be people like myself, other people who are blind, visually impaired and other people with disabilities just continuing to push and say if we're going to continue spending money here and coming to your businesses we need to see more things made accessible."

articles.title: European skies on high alert after hoax bomb threats this week – Europe live
articles.summary:
Hoax bomb threats targeted commercial flights this week leaving at least 35 planes searched or diverted

Airlines and airports across Europe are on high alert after a wave of hoax…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 26m agoMorning opening: European skies on high alert after hoax bomb threats this week

blocks.text: Morning opening: European skies on high alert after hoax bomb threats this week

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Airlines and airports across Europe are on high alert after a wave of hoax bomb threats targeted commercial flights this week, leaving at least 35 planes searched or diverted.
Authorities will be hoping to see a quieter day today after yesterday’s disruptions.
But one of the incidents yesterday remains under closer scrutiny.

An Aer Lingus pilot who was flying from Dublin to Rome when the plane was diverted to the Évreux military base after a bomb threat is facing scrutiny from the French authorities after reportedly insisting on landing at a civilian airport.

blocks.caption: An Aer Lingus aircraft which was heading from Dublin to Rome and has been rerouted and escorted by military aircraft after a suspected bomb threat at Evreux-Fauville Air Base. Photograph: Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Évreux’s public prosecutor, Rémi Coutin, told ICI Normandie that the pilot’s apparent initial refusal to land where instructed prompted the French military to scramble two fighter jets to intercept the aircraft.
The pilot and his co-pilot will be questioned to “understand what happened,” Coutin said, stressing that he could bring charges for refusing to cooperate with authorities.
In a statement to the Guardian, Aer Lingus backed the pilot, however, saying he and the crew acted “impeccably and thoroughly professional throughout” the incident.

“Safety and the care of our passengers is Aer Lingus’ top priority and this was upheld professionally by the captain and crew of the aircraft throughout in what were very challenging circumstances,” the airline said.
Elsewhere, we are expecting an update on the Belgian government as prime minister Bart De Wever meets King Philippe to discuss next steps after the collapse of budget negotiations.
Pope Leo is also off to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in his first overseas trip since his lung surgery last month.
I will bring you all the updates here.
It’s Friday, 6 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Is The Pitt an unauthorized ER reboot? Court approves lawsuit alleging yes
articles.summary: There are so many similarities between the hit TV series ER and HBO's The Pitt that a lawsuit should be allowed to proceed, a U.S. appeals court ruled Wednesday. The lawsuit was filed by the widow of…

image.caption: Michael Crichton created ER, right, in the 1990s based on a film script he wrote about his experiences as a medical student. His widow Sherri says there are so many similarities with The Pitt, left, that the 2025 series should be considered an unauthorized reboot. (HBO, 2001 Warner Bros. Internation

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

There are so many similarities between the hit TV series ER and HBO's The Pitt that a lawsuit should be allowed to proceed, a U.S. appeals court ruled Wednesday. The lawsuit was filed by the widow of Michael Crichton, who created the TV series ER in the 1990s, based on a film script he wrote about his time as a medical student.
Star Noah Wyle, executive producer and showrunner dropped as defendants
There are so many similarities between the hit TV series ER and HBO's The Pitt that a lawsuit should be allowed to proceed, a U.S. appeals court ruled Wednesday.
The lawsuit was filed by Sherri Crichton, widow of Michael Crichton, who created the TV series ER in the 1990s based on a film script he wrote about his time as a medical student.

He died in 2008. But in 1994, when he signed a contract with Warner Bros. Television for ER, it explicitly said no spin-offs or reboots could be made without his — or his estate's — approval, according to documents filed in the Court of Appeal of the State of California.
In her initial lawsuit, Sherri Crichton says she engaged in negotiations to develop a reboot in 2022, but they were unable to reach an agreement.
Warner Bros. continued to develop The Pitt anyway.
Crichton filed a lawsuit against Warner Bros. alleging The Pitt was an unauthorized reboot in August 2024, nearly five months before the new series debuted.
In August 2025, Warner Bros. filed a motion to dismiss Crichton's lawsuit, citing California’s anti-SLAPP legislation, designed to protect citizens from lawsuits that target free speech.
A judge denied the motion, so the defendants took it to a California appeals court.

items: The Pitt and other medical shows finally acknowledge 'backbone' of health care: Filipino nurses

blocks.text: Noah Wyle, John Wells and R. Scott Gemmill were also named as defendants. Wyle stars in both TV series, while Wells is the executive producer of both ER and The Pitt. Gemmill, who is The Pitt's showrunner, also briefly worked as executive producer of ER.
In their appeal, the defendants argue The Pitt is a "brand-new medical drama with no ties to ER."
They say their show has "different characters, settings, visuals, styles, music, timing, and more."
ER was set in Chicago, and The Pitt is set in Pittsburgh.
So what exactly do the two shows have in common, other than Wyle?
A panel of three judges at the California appeals court, in their unanimous opinion rejecting the defendants' appeal, said both TV series:

items: Are medical dramas set in emergency departments.
Feature dialogue full of medical jargon.
Portray overlapping crises and graphic depictions of injuries.
Portray exhausted doctors and nurses.
Contain frequent emotional outbursts.
Include a young doctor, fresh from medical school and incompetent.

blocks.text: The appeals court also ruled on Wednesday that Warner Bros. must go to trial, but Wyle, Wells and Gemmill have been dismissed as defendants — as it found no evidence they were aware they could violate Crichton's contractual rights.
Unless the parties reach a settlement, the suit will go to a jury trial in Los Angeles.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Worst of beef price hikes may be over, but don’t expect cheaper steak anytime soon
articles.summary: Beef prices are at record highs. But there is some good news for Canadians who enjoy a good steak. Beef prices have stabilized, but experts say that doesn't mean grocery prices will be dropping…

image.caption: Beef is cut at Ben's Quality Meats, a processing facility in Picture Butte, Alta. Canada's cattle herd is beginning to recover after years of declining numbers but experts say high production costs will keep beef prices elevated. (Monty Kruger/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Beef prices are at record highs. But there is some good news for Canadians who enjoy a good steak. Beef prices have stabilized, but experts say that doesn't mean grocery prices will be dropping anytime soon.
Canada's cattle herd is growing and prices are stabilizing, but experts warn little relief for consumers
After years of soaring beef prices, Canadians may finally be getting a break from steep price increases when buying their favourite cut of steak or roast at the grocery store.
Beef prices rose 8.7 per cent in September compared with a year earlier and have climbed 55.5 per cent over the past five years, according to Statistics Canada.
Prices remain at record highs, but industry experts say there are signs of stability, with grocery store price tags remaining relatively flat for much of 2026.
"The worst of the price jumps I would say are over," said Brenna Grant, executive director of Calgary-based beef statistics firm Canfax.
"We've had some really big price jumps in the last four years and any change going forward is going to be more moderate."
Brenna Grant, executive director of Canfax, says the worst of the beef price spikes may be over, but Canadians shouldn't expect prices to drop significantly. (Ina Sidhu/CBC)
Cattle supplies growing
Canada's cattle herd is growing after years of declining numbers.
Statistics Canada reported 12.1 million cattle and calves on Canadian farms as of July 1, 2026, up 3.2 per cent from a year earlier, the largest annual increase since 2004.

items: Beef prices are soaring. Here's why Canada is facing record-low cattle numbers
Grilling pains: Why your BBQ may cost more this summer

blocks.text: The industry has struggled with years of drought in Western Canada and the U.S. Midwest, rising feed costs and shrinking herds.
In southern Alberta, rancher Michael Munton is seeing a shift.
Munton operates Benchmark Angus near Warner, Alta., as well as a processing facility in Picture Butte, Alta.
"This summer prices were the highest that anyone has ever seen in the beef market and we're starting to see that come down," he said.
Munton said ranchers are working to expand their herds but face factors beyond their control.
"All of it is contingent on weather providing that we have good moisture this winter and in the spring, then we should be able to see some stability in that market," Munton said.
He said dry conditions could force producers to sell cattle and set back the recovery.

Cattle stand in a feedlot in southern Alberta. Canada’s cattle herd is growing after years of declining numbers, but experts warn it could take time before consumers see price relief at the grocery store. (Ina Sidhu/CBC)
Why beef could stay expensive in 2027
Experts say consumers shouldn't expect a significant drop in prices at the meat counter.
Kevin Grier, a livestock market analyst based in Guelph, Ont., said North American beef supplies remain tight, while demand has held up despite record prices.
"The only so-called hope of getting lower prices is if all of a sudden Canadian consumers decide that they don't want beef and then therefore the demand declines," he said.

Grier cautioned that North American cattle supplies could become even tighter in 2027 as ranchers hold back breeding animals. That means fewer cattle going to slaughter in the short term, even as producers work to increase supply over the longer term.
Whether that pushes beef prices up will depend on consumer demand, he said.

Stephen Deere is the owner of Modern Steak in Calgary. He says soaring beef prices are putting pressure on restaurant margins and changing how some customers order, with some opting to skip an appetizer or side dish to enjoy their favourite steak. (Ina Sidhu/CBC)
That appetite for beef is also holding up at restaurants.
At Modern Steak in Calgary, owner Stephen Deere said high beef prices are squeezing profits and have forced him to raise menu prices by as much as 10 per cent this year.
"No one wants to do it, it's the last resort," he said. "At the end of the day when you're a prime-grade steakhouse, it's prime-grade beef. There is no substitution for that."
Deere said diners aren't necessarily giving up their favourite steaks but finding other ways to keep bills down.
"I don't see too many people downsizing their regular order. Meaning if I order a rib eye I'm still ordering a rib eye," said Deere.
"What they're doing is they might have one less appetizer, one less side or one less drink."
Are high beef prices the new normal?

Michael Munton is the owner and operator of Benchmark Angus in southern Alberta. He says Canadian cattle herds are expanding after years of drought — but continued growth will depend on favourable weather conditions for grazing land. (Ina Sidhu/CBC News)
Even as cattle supplies recover, experts say beef prices are unlikely to return to what Canadians paid several years ago.
For ranchers, the economics of producing beef have changed dramatically.
"The cost of the infrastructure, the cost of the machinery, the cost of the equipment is astronomical. And the margins that we live on are very, very slim," Munton said.
Those rising costs extend throughout the entire supply chain, including fuel and transportation, according to Grant, and have changed the economics of producing beef.
"It's very rare that you actually see those retail prices come down in any significant way," Grant said.
"Any relief would be very modest and it may be on only some cuts."

articles.title: Global stocks plunge amid AI slowdown fears after Democrats’ midterm triumph
articles.summary: Asian and European markets follow Wall Street with sharp fall as FTSE down 1.5%

blocks.text: European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, with the FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, down 1.5%, or 166 points, at the start of trading to 10,615.

The pharmaceuticals company AstraZeneca opened down 2.8%, the biggest faller on the FTSE 100. Other big fallers included IAG, the owner of British Airways and Iberia, which fell 1.5%, after it missed profit forecasts in a trading update, and the miners Antofagasta and Anglo American.
Germany’s Dax index opened down 1.5%, France’s Cac 40 has dropped by 1.2% and Spain’s Ibex is down 1.1%.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe.

“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.

Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8% in early trading.
Despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year.
after newsletter promotion
The Nasdaq Composite index, for example, is still up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.

articles.title: Employers to be forced to put salaries on job ads, Andy Burnham announces
articles.summary: Workers’ rights campaigners say measure will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay

blocks.text: Employers will be forced to publish salaries on job adverts, Andy Burnham has announced, in an effort to empower both employees and jobseekers.

The prime minister said his government would bring in a legal requirement for companies to say what they pay when listing new jobs, which campaigners say will help young people and women in particular achieve more equal pay.

Burnham said the move would help deal with the frustration of applying for a job without knowing the salary, while officials say that publicising pay will help those in work know if they are being paid fairly in comparison with others.

The prime minister said: “Whether you’re a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it. That’s why we will make it a legal requirement for all employers to say what you pay.

“But breaking down barriers is only one part of the job. We also need businesses to open more doors and give young people the experience and confidence to take that first step into the world of work.”
Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, said: “Anyone who’s searched for a job knows how frustrating it is to read ‘competitive salary’.”

Burnham has spent much of his first few months in power announcing a series of “small fixes” to help improve people’s daily lives, while promising more radical change to come. The changes have included removing VAT from electricity bills, reducing bus fares and a £100 council tax rebate announced at the budget.

The prime minister is working on a 10-year plan for ending what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism”, which is expected to include more fundamental reforms such as bringing utilities under public control. He said this week the plan could be delayed until next year, having originally been expected next month.

Ministers first consulted in July on a series of moves to improve how existing equal pay laws work. That document also proposed greater equality protections for disabled people and ethnic minorities, but ministers have not yet set out their final plans on those points.
They have promised further policy changes to help young people into work in response to a review by the former minister Alan Milburn in the coming weeks.
after newsletter promotion

Recent research by the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found less than half of employers always published salaries ranges on job adverts, while less than a fifth always published specific salaries.

Experts say omitting pay details from job adverts makes it harder for young people to know which jobs to apply for, and makes it easier for employers to give lower pay offers to some candidates, including women.

The government said 93% of businesses responded positively to the consultation. Ministers have not yet decided exactly what information will have to be published, which size of company will have to comply, or how it will be enforced.

articles.title: Pope Leo sets off on 12-day South America tour
articles.summary: The pontiff will hold meetings and celebrate Mass in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, with the latter attracting particular interest. The trip will be the longest and farthest of his papacy so far.

image.caption: The pope took off from Rome's Fiumicino airport in the early hours of the morningImage: Filippo Monteforte/AFP

blocks.text: The plane carrying Pope Leo XIV to South America for the beginning of his almost two-week tour set off from Rome on Friday.
Following a 13-and-a-half-hour flight, the pontiff is set to land in Uruguay, where he will spend three days before heading on to Argentina, and finally Peru.
The 71-year-old US-born pope is recovering from a lung cancer surgery that took place just three weeks ago.
Latin America is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, for whom the pope is their spiritual leader. However, fewer and fewer people on the continent identify as Catholic.
What is Pope Leo planning for his visit to Uruguay?
Pope Leo's first leg of the tour takes him to Uruguay, the most secular Latin American country.
It was the first country in the world to legalize recreational marijuana use and has since legalized abortion, same-sex marriage and assisted dying, all against opposition from the Catholic Church.
However, the enthusiasm around Leo's visit has come as a bit of a surprise, with tickets for his prayer vigil at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium selling out in just two days.

blocks.caption: The pope is expected to express opposition to some of the more liberal policies enacted in UruguayImage: Lucas Aguayo Araos/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: The trip will begin with a meeting with President Yamandu Orsi, leader of a center-left alliance. He is also planning to visit the Casavalle neighborhood, which is notorious for its high rates of poverty and violence.
With the first papal visit to Uruguay since 1988, Leo will be hoping to reinvigorate the faith in a country where only a fraction of believers attend Mass.
What will Pope Leo do in Argentina?
On Sunday, Leo will cross over to neighboring Argentina, the home of his papal predecessor Francis, who, however, disappointed his native compatriots by never returning home as pope.
At the beginning of Francis's papacy, some 71% of Argentinians identified as Catholic, according to the Pew Research Center. By 2024, this had fallen to 58%.

blocks.caption: Leo will hope his visit makes up for the refusal by his predecessor to visit his home countryImage: Agustin Marcarian/REUTERS

blocks.text: Leo is set to meet with Argentinian President Javier Milei, who has come under criticism from the Catholic Church for his sweeping cuts that have hampered programs for the poor and needy.
He is also planning to meet with business leaders, trade unions, workers and social representatives.
Pope Leo to return to Peru
The final leg of the trip, on Wednesday, will see Leo return to Peru, where he lived and preached for two decades.
There is excitement about his visit to Peru, with the pope planning to celebrate Mass in his old diocese of Chiclayo as well as in the mountain village of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba.
The pope will also celebrate Mass in the former Incan capital city of Cusco before honoring Peru's indigenous population by traveling to Pucallpa in the Peruvian Amazon.
The excitement can be seen in the street vendors selling T-shirts and rosaries with his likeness, while bakeries have been selling Leo bread.
Peru has also seen a weakening of the faithful in recent years, with the Catholic population falling from 76% in 2013-2014 to around 67% now.

blocks.caption: Peruvian Catholics have shown particular interest in the pope's visit as a type of homecomingImage: Martin Mejia/AP Photo/picture alliance

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte 'saddened, very angered' by manhunt vs. allies, says Kitty
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte has expressed disapproval of what he perceives as efforts of the Marcos administration to go after his allies and supporters instead of addressing the needs of the…

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 4:41pm

Former president Rodrigo Duterte has expressed disapproval of what he perceives as efforts of the Marcos administration to go after his allies and supporters instead of addressing the needs of the nation, his daughter Veronica “Kitty” Duterte said.

“He is saddened and very angered by the fact that the taxpayers' money is being focused sa pagpadakop sa kanang mga kaalyado nato, mga supporters, instead of the more important things,” Kitty Duterte said in a mix of English and Bisaya in an interview posted on the Facebook page of Alvin & Tourism.
(He is saddened and very angry by the fact that the taxpayers' money is being focused on arresting his allies and supporters, instead of the more important things.)

“Like right now, may El Niño, ‘di ba (there’s El Niño, right)? And several other things like flood control projects, budgets for the more important things, for the needs, the basic needs of the Filipino people,” she added.
The Philippine government has raised a P50-million reward for the arrest of Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, one of the known allies of the former president.
Dela Rosa has been issued an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in relation to the drug war of the Duterte administration, which supposedly killed thousands of people.
He was the chief of the Philippine National Police at the time the controversial anti-drug campaign was implemented.
Duterte, meanwhile, is currently detained at the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands, while awaiting his crimes against humanity trial.
Kitty Duterte said that Filipinos should stand firm in their convictions in opposing the supposed injustices in the Philippines.

“All I can say is that now more than ever, we have to remain steadfast in our conviction and on our stand against all the injustices we are facing as a people, as a nation, because we are the only ones who can stop this,” she said.
“At some point, it will get too much. So it depends on us,” she added. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Bojie Dy, the unexciting Speaker whom Marcos can count on
articles.summary: Rappler takes an inside look into the speakership of Bojie Dy, and paints a picture of a man who holds the country's fourth top job yet contends with the limits of his power

blocks.text: The story goes that when Speaker Bojie Dy needs to talk to Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, or vice versa, it’s the 65-year-old Isabela gentleman, the country’s fourth-highest official, who goes down to the office of the President’s son, not the other way around.

It’s a peculiar visual, confirmed in private to Rappler by two congressional sources who have personal knowledge about the two leaders’ dynamic. “It’s the mountain that comes to Mohammed,” one of them quipped.

More than a year into his speakership, Dy has mostly avoided the weight of the scandals that crushed his predecessor Martin Romualdez. He enjoys a sterling reputation among his colleagues, and even clashing voices agree he’s a nice guy.
But he also carries the enduring perception of playing second fiddle to the son of the commander-in-chief.
His speakership comes with the mighty title. But is the actual power sold separately?

blocks.caption: Bojie Dy

blocks.text: Dy was not top of mind to become the new House speaker. By August 2025, it was becoming clear to Malacañang that the flood control fiasco had exhausted Romualdez’s remaining political capital, and he had to go.

Those initially in contention to replace him were Navotas’ Toby Tiangco, Bataan’s Abet Garcia, and Bacolod’s Albee Benitez. Garcia and Benitez reportedly did not pass the Palace’s vetting, while Tiangco had already publicly said he did not want the chamber’s top post.

Dy’s name only came up later, but the choice made sense. He already belongs to the President’s Partido Federal ng Pilipinas, and was even the first PFP lawmaker to be included in Romualdez’s deputy speaker roster for the 20th Congress.

He was also seen as nonpolarizing. He wasn’t angling for the speakership or seen as politically ambitious or selfish. The Isabela native was just returning to the House after spending 15 years as governor and vice governor.

Dy may have come from a political family that lorded over Cagayan Valley’s largest economy for decades — 16 relatives are currently in government — but he did not have the same connections that made Romualdez a powerhouse in Congress.
Dy, nonetheless, was obviously the safe choice for speaker by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., as both of their families go way back, and the two share the “Solid North” regional bond.
Dy’s father, the late patriarch of their dynasty, was a loyal ally of dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos. Dy was already active in the Kabataang Barangay (KB) during the Martial Law regime.

“Though he was from a very influential political family while I was from humble roots, we got along well because as always he was down to earth, kind, and soft spoken,” Caloocan 2nd District Representative Edgar Erice, Dy’s KB contemporary, told Rappler.
In 2016, Dy backed Marcos Jr.’s failed bid for the vice presidency, and again in 2022, when the dictator’s son successfully reclaimed Malacañang.
As speaker, Romualdez was always seen as the President’s reliable shield against any impeachment attempt. When his time was up, Marcos needed another loyal ally. Dy fit the bill.

“We see no basis that would justify the impeachment complaint filed against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.,” Dy said as soon as a petition against Marcos reached the House for the first time earlier this year.

blocks.caption: Who is Faustino ‘Bojie’ Dy, successor of Martin Romualdez as House speaker?

blocks.text: On Day 1 of Dy’s leadership in September 2025, he made a commitment to clean up Congress’ ranks. “We have fallen short,” he admitted.

Dy had two main tasks: calm an electorate frustrated with corruption in Congress, and ease the anxiety of lawmakers who feared they were the next target of the administration’s supposed anti-graft campaign.
Whether he succeeded in both is another story.

This was the height of the scandal, when dozens of lawmakers were being exposed for their alleged ties to construction firms that undertake public works projects for hundreds of millions — if not billions — of pesos.
Zaldy Co. Edwin Gardiola. Dong Gonzales. Chiz Escudero. The Dutertes. The Villars.

“Speaker Dy told lawmakers at the time, let’s trust the process. If you’re not involved and have nothing to worry about, let the process take its course,” Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez, Dy’s closest House ally, said.

blocks.caption: TRACKER: Public officials with links to government contractors

blocks.text: Dy oversaw the abolition of the small committee, a closed-door group that decided which budget amendments to accept even after the House had passed the spending bill.

The Dy-led House instead livestreamed budget amendment deliberations to show more transparency. But watchdogs it supposedly partnered with remained dissatisfied, and called efforts an “empty gesture.”

The House’s 2026 budget reportedly added P23 billion for public works. Dy’s district was a top recipient, with funding more than tripled to P3.8 billion from P1.1 billion. For 2027, public works allocations for his district stand at P3.1 billion.

“We were asked to sacrifice, yet their districts were the ones that benefited,” House Deputy Speaker Ronnie Puno, president of the House’s second largest bloc National Unity Party, said in March 2026, when he publicly criticized the House leadership over budget woes.
Puno’s callout of the Speaker underscored Dy’s limited power to give Congress a fresh start after the budget scandal.

blocks.caption: WATCH: Why the budget process of Philippine Congress is prone to corruption

blocks.text: When Dy became speaker, he retained all of Romualdez’s deputy speakers and added five more, inflating the roster. He also kept Romualdez’s budget chair, Mika Suansing.

Unlike Romualdez, Dy is not perceived as the epicenter of power in the House. It’s the President’s son, the 32-year-old Sandro, who has become an unstoppable force in the chamber, according to numerous lawmakers whom Rappler spoke with.

“If a congressman has needs for his district, they are more comfortable reaching out to Sandro than the Speaker,” one lawmaker from the majority, speaking on condition of anonymity, explained, citing Sandro’s direct line to the Palace.
“Sandro has become politically mature, unlike before when he played a more background role.”

blocks.caption: 2026 BUDGET. Speaker Bojie Dy and Majority Leader Sandro Marcos pose for a photo op with other House lawmakers after it passes the proposed 2026 budget in October 2025. Photo from Sandro Marcos’ Facebook

blocks.text: Another lawmaker said that Sandro, with all the power he commands, needs Dy and his candor to soften the message.

“There are some lawmakers who find Sandro to be abrasive sometimes,” the second source said. “Si Bojie ang taga-areglo, taga-masahe (Bojie is the one who smoothens things out and acts as a mediator).”
Kamanggagawa Representative Eli San Fernando recalled his lobbying efforts on the abolition of provincial wage rates. It hasn’t borne fruit despite support from Dy and over 200 lawmakers.
“The logical thing is for Majority Leader Sandro to schedule it for plenary consideration. But he doesn’t, because the Palace and the economic managers do not want to,” San Fernando said.

Senior Deputy Speaker Hernandez thinks the Speaker has more agency than what the public sees. “It is unfair to say that because the Majority Leader is the son of the President, the Speaker will lie low. The Speaker is just quiet, but the President talks to the Speaker directly,” Hernandez said.

blocks.caption: TRUST. President Marcos and Speaker Dy speak on the sidelines of a Palace event. Photo from Dy’s Facebook

blocks.text: Other deputy speakers speak positively of Dy, who is often described as “humble.”
“He is a good person, amicable and very down to earth. He is always available,” Deputy Speaker Benitez told Rappler.

“He goes around without a retinue of camp followers, and his office in the House is not a closed, exclusive private club of privilege, but open to all representatives and to the people,’” Deputy Speaker Raymond Mendoza said in a separate text message to Rappler.
The unspoken limitations of the title that Dy holds complicate any effort to leave a personal legacy.

His flagship initiative is LegisHear, a program intended to bring Congress closer to the people. It involves lawmakers going to the provinces to hear their constituents out and help shape future legislation.
But is the House under his leadership effective in its lawmaking function?
In the first year of the 20th Congress from July 2025 to July 2026, out of his 52 pet bills, President Marcos enacted only one — the resetting of the Bangsamoro elections.

Almost half of these proposals had already hurdled the House, but the Senate — plagued by infighting and leadership coups — has become a bottleneck. Many measures, even those considered a priority, were pushed to the backburner.

blocks.caption: Marcos ends fourth year with fewer enacted pet bills to brag about

blocks.text: These factors have left the Speaker little to no tangible legislation to brag about.

The stalled proposals include the House bills on freedom of information, much-criticized anti-disinformation, the widely welcomed travel tax abolition, institutionalizing the government’s social amelioration program AICS, and the diluted anti-dynasty legislation.
The Speaker’s Kalinga bill, meant to ease fuel-driven inflation, found no strong Senate champion. Of what good is a meritorious House bill if no senator will carry it across the finish line?
Rappler has written to Dy’s office, asking for a sit-down interview. It has not been granted as of writing.

blocks.caption: Bojie Dy, the unexciting Speaker whom Marcos can count on

blocks.text: These days, there has been loose talk of Dy being a strong candidate for the vice presidency, should Sara Duterte be convicted at the impeachment court.
Dy is said to have played a passive role in the entire impeachment saga, despite being head of the chamber that enabled her trial at the Senate.

Hernandez claimed that even Dy didn’t know the final tally on the day of the May impeachment vote, only that there were enough numbers to indict the Vice President. At the trial, Dy delegated the task of managing the prosecutors to Deputy Speaker Jayjay Suarez.
The Constitution states that when the vice presidency is vacated, the President shall nominate a replacement from among the members of the Senate and the House.
Dy has not publicly declared his intent for the job, and likely won’t. Even his closest allies call him a reluctant speaker who never chased the post many of his colleagues covet.

“I’m not endorsing anyone, but he’s kind. BBM will sleep soundly if he is the vice president,” Navotas Representative Toby Tiangco told Rappler, when asked about what he thinks of Dy as a potential veep.
“Whether he will be a good VP to the Filipino people remains to be seen but he definitely will be a good VP to the President,” Erice added.

The vice presidency isn’t Dy’s to lose in this world of what-ifs. For him to get it, Duterte must first be removed, rumored rivals (Chiz Escudero, Win Gatchalian, Tito Sotto, even Lito Lapid) must step aside, and he must be offered the post and accept it.
For a man whose influence has been doubted, maybe the idea that he is being considered, has the agency to say yes or no, and has the opportunity to be reluctant, is power in itself. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Malaysia: Jailed ex-leader Najib to leave prison for house arrest
articles.summary: Convicted in the 1MDB scandal for embezzling millions, jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak will serve his prison term under house arrest after his party had collected donations to pay his fine.

image.caption: Najib, center, was sentenced to a separate 15-year sentence after a marathon trial in December 2025Image: Mohd Rasfan/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Malaysia's graft-convicted former Prime Minister Najib Razak is set to leave prison to sit out the remainder of a six-year sentence under house arrest, after his political party paid a 50 million ringgit ($12.3 million, €11 million) fine.
Najib's party, United Malays National Organization (UMNO), collected sufficient funds through a donation drive, Asyraf Wajid Dusuki, the party secretary-general, said in a statement on Friday.

Although it was not immediately clear when Najib would be officially allowed to leave prison, the AFP news agency said a report sa him in a car driving away on Friday. Police were stationed at his house in Kuala Lumpur early Friday and the road leading to his home was blocked.
Billions stolen from state funds

Najib, 73, has been serving a six-year prison sentence for his role in the 1MDB corruption scandal, named after 1Malaysia Development Berhad, a state investment fund he co-founded while serving as prime minister from 2009 to 2018.

In 2020, Najib was originally sentenced to 12 years in prison for abuse of power, criminal breach of trust and money laundering involving $10.3 million funneled into his bank accounts. He began his sentence in 2022.

blocks.caption: The Jailed ex-prime minister is still influential in his partyImage: Mohd Rasfan/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Malaysia's king, Sultan Ibrahim, granted Najib a rare royal clemency in September, subject to the payment of 50 million Malaysian ringgit, allowing him to serve the rest of his sentence under house arrest.
Second prison sentence awaiting
The house arrest applies only to his reduced six-year sentence in the first trial.
It doesn't cover a separate 15-year prison sentence imposed in December 2025 for corruption and money laundering in a second trial tied to the 1MDB scandal.
Malaysia's former PM guilty in major corruption scandal
Najib is appealing that conviction, which saw him fined 11.4 billion ringgit.
If he fails to win the appeal, he could go back to prison after August 23, 2028.

The scandal sparked national outrage in Malaysia and led to the 2018 election defeat of Najib's party United Malays National Organization (UNMO), which governed the country since independence from Britain in 1957.
In spite of the embezzlement, Najib still enjoys political support and is influential in this party, which is part of the government that came to power in 2022.

articles.title: 2 at-large suspects in Bacoor shootout identified --PNP chief
articles.summary: Two suspects who remain at large following a shootout in Bacoor, Cavite, which left five people dead, have already been identified, Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Melencio…

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 4:29pm

Two suspects who remain at large following a shootout in Bacoor, Cavite that left five people dead have already been identified, Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Friday.
In an ambush interview, Nartatez said police are now pursuing the two suspects who managed to evade arrest during the operation on Tuesday.
“Yung dalawa (Regarding the two at-large suspects), police are now hot on the trail of these two suspects. They were already identified,” Nartatez said in an ambush interview.
Five of the seven suspected members of the Gapos Gang syndicate were killed in the armed encounter with the Bacoor City Police on Tuesday in Barangay Molino.
The suspects were allegedly members of a robbery group that had been under police surveillance for its involvement in several robbery incidents and other crimes.
According to the police, the group had planned to enter a subdivision or residential area while posing as security guards.
The group allegedly intended to rob a businessman believed to be keeping valuable items and a substantial amount of money at his residence.
Police chased the suspects as they fled aboard a car and a motorcycle after they were spotted lurking near their target subdivision around noon. The sedan overturned during the chase.
Two of the five suspects killed in the shootout with cops were former police officers, according to the PNP.
Nartatez said investigators will also determine whether the suspects were involved in other criminal activities in the past.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Death a ‘distinct possibility’ in collision running and face-slapping competitions, inquiry hears
articles.summary:
Impacts in emerging contact sports are akin to coward punches and cannot be made safer with regulation, neurologist says

  • Get our

blocks.text: Collision running and face-slapping competitions have similar impacts to that of a coward punch or “king-hit”, with death a “distinct possibility”, a concussion expert has told a parliamentary inquiry.

A New South Wales inquiry is examining whether emerging competitions such as Run Nation, in which two players run at each other and collide at high speed, and Power Slap, where players take turns slapping each other across the face, should be considered combat sports to better regulate the safety of participants.

But neurologist Dr Rowena Mobbs, an expert in concussion and chronic traumatic encepalopahty (CTE), told the inquiry she did not think there was “any form of modification” that would make the sports safer.
“Collision running and Power Slap are worse than eye-gouging and should be deemed a king-hit, for death is a distinct possibility,” she said.

A 19-year-old died in New Zealand last year after suffering a critical head injury playing a tackling game believed to have been inspired by the viral “run it straight” challenge, of which Run Nation’s organisers have claimed their competition is a safer version, turning rugby league “hit-ups” into a sport.

The inquiry was established in August. In September, a NSW supreme court judge ruled Run Nation was a combat sport, upholding a cancellation notice for a Sydney event that month from the Combat Sports Authority (CSA) of NSW.
The event has been rescheduled for 28 November after the authority’s medical advisory board approved its permit. Power Slap has yet to host an official event in Australia.
The chair of the CSA, Darren Kane, told the inquiry on Friday he would prefer to see new combat sports regulated, with mandated ambulance and medical support staff.

“If it was a regulated event, there’d be all these systems in place, and the people would have accreditations, they would have done concussion training, there would be doctors mandated at the events,” he said.
“Whereas you have these unregulated things, it’s pot luck.”
Run Nation’s organisers have said their events include on-field doctors and paramedics.
The inquiry did not hear from organisers of either competition, but received submissions from medical experts, bareknuckle boxing and grassroots combat sports groups.

Petero Taremwa, the founder of Get That Guap (GTG) fight club, which hosts mixed martial arts, kickboxing and boxing fights without a promoter’s licence, said the cost of participation was a “serious barrier” to fighters, while organisers faced significant costs from “permits, insurance, venues, and medical services”.
after newsletter promotion
“We’re not here to dispute the importance of regulation. We’re here because we want a realistic pathway to comply,” he said.
Taremwa said there had been no significant injuries at GTG events, which “always had a nurse who is also our DJ, who looks at the fighters right after the fight”.

Under questioning from the inquiry chair, Labor MLC Sarah Kaine, Taremwa said he did not think he knew better than the CSA, but that the cost of on-site ambulances required under regulation was unreasonable for an entry-level organiser.

In her evidence, Mobbs said brain diseases in participants in football codes and traditional combat sports resulted from “subclinical concussions or silent events … when they add up to probably tens of thousands if not hundreds of thousands”.

But she said the stronger impacts experienced in collision running and face-slapping competitions meant a lower number of impacts could “trigger off a neurodegenerative disease, for example, later in life”.
Mobbs said she did not recall treating any patients with injuries from collision running or Power Slap.
She likened the potential impact to that of a coward punch or “king-hit”, because participants could not defend themselves and strikes came “right in the key area where you have most impact”.
The inquiry is expected to report back in December.

articles.title: Somalia's top court rejects president's term extension amid political crisis
articles.summary: The country's first nationwide elections since 1969 are due next year - a timetable now thrown into doubt.

blocks.text: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.
Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.
The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.
Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.
Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule.
But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives.
Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabaab controlling many rural areas.
On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.
In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.
The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.
The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary.
But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach.

The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.
Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency.
"Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.
AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.
The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.

The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.
Mohamud has called for national talks from 14 to 18 November to resolve the deadlock, but opposition leaders have questioned his legitimacy to convene the discussions.
The political turmoil comes as Somalia continues to battle al-Shabaab, which controls large parts of the countryside despite years of military operations.

Uganda, the largest contributor of troops to the African Union mission fighting the militants, announced this week that it planned to withdraw its forces by the end of the year, adding to concerns about Somalia's security.

blocks.caption: 'Königreich Deutschland' or 'Kingdom of Germany' is accused of trying to set up a 'counter state'Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four alleged ringleaders of the banned far-right "Kingdom of Germany" (KRD) are expected to appear before the Düsseldorf Higher Regional Court this morning.
The group is part of a conspiracy theorist movement that rejects the legitimacy of the modern German republic.

Authorities banned the KRD in May 2025 after monitoring its activities for more than a decade. Since then, the four defendants, including the group's so-called "King" Peter Fitzek, have been held in pre-trial detention.
They have been charged with membership in a criminal organization and other offenses, including document forgery and tax evasion amounting to millions of euros.

The Federal Prosecutor's Office accuses Fitzek and his co-defendants of seeking to replace the German republic with their own system. They are alleged to have set up "pseudo-state structures" such as a banking and insurance system, as well as a "registration office" that issued fictitious identity documents.

At the time the group was banned, hundreds of police officers carried out raids on 15 properties across Germany. They seized "further evidence of the association's anti-constitutional goals and activities," according to the Interior Ministry.
Authorities said the group had acquired land through donations with the aim of reducing the territory of Germany.
According to the prosecutor's office, they sought to expand their purported territory to the borders of the German Empire of 1871.
The group is estimated to have had around 1,000 followers at the time it was banned.
