articles.title: Senate impeachment court reimposes gag order for withdrawn articles
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court has reimposed its gag order on the three charges prosecutors dropped against Vice President Sara Duterte, reversing an October ruling that had freed both sides to discuss…

blocks.text: November 6, 2026 | 10:58am
(From L) Impeachment defense counsels Sheila Sison and Michael Poa, lead prosecutor Rep. Jinky Luistro, Sen. Pia Cayetano and presiding officer Chiz Escudero and private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan.
Senate SMU / Joseph Vidal

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court has reimposed its gag order on the three charges prosecutors dropped against Vice President Sara Duterte, reversing an October ruling that had freed both sides to discuss them in public.

In an order issued on Friday, Nov. 6, the court said the sub judice ban under Rule XVIII of its trial rules applies "with equal force" to all four articles of impeachment, whether withdrawn or still pending.

The aim of the rule is to prevent any side from "litigating dropped charges in the media" while senator-judges try the one remaining charge, Article II, which accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth.

The order resolves a motion for reconsideration that Sen. Kiko Pangilinan raised on October 13. It also follows a November 4 manifestation in which Duterte told the court she was not waiving the rule and wanted the ban kept in place.
The House prosecutors withdrew Articles I, III and IV on October 13, during the trial's 39th day, after the prosecution had formally rested its case.

The dropped articles covered the alleged misuse of confidential funds at the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education, alleged bribery of DepEd officials, and threats Duterte allegedly made against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.

Escudero accepted the withdrawal, and in doing so, had then lifted the sub judice rule on all three dropped articles, reasoning that since Duterte no longer had to answer them in court, she should be free to answer them in public. However, lead defense counsel Sheila Sison objected on the spot, warning that it would open the door to "unregulated and unbridled" public statements against the vice president.
Pangilinan then moved for reconsideration. In response, Escudero held off acting on the motion until the defense formally stated Duterte's position.

Violators of the restored ban face the penalties Escudero laid down on August 26, when the court cleared parties of earlier breaches but promised strict enforcement from then on. A first offense draws a severe reprimand in open court, entered into the record as a final warning. Later violations can bring a fine of up to P30,000 each, limits on an offending lawyer's right to speak, object or question witnesses, and referral to the Integrated Bar of the Philippines and the Supreme Court.

In a companion ruling released the same day, the court acted on the prosecution's formal offer of evidence for Article II. It excluded in full the Commission on Audit records on confidential-fund disallowances at the OVP and DepEd, saying exhibits tied to Article I cannot be re-offered under Article II because that charge was withdrawn with prejudice.
Duterte, who has denied wrongdoing, begins presenting her defense on Monday, November 9.

articles.title: What prediction markets told us about the midterm election
articles.summary: While Kalshi and Polymarket hail big wins for their accurate midterm markets, experts say they missed out on historic and surprise wins.

image.caption: A screen displays a Kalshi advertisement on political betting featuring Senate control in New York City, in late October. (Jeenah Moon/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business
While Kalshi and Polymarket hail big wins for their accurate midterm markets, experts say they missed out on historic and surprise wins.
Experts say the markets accurately predicted major races but failed to foresee a Democratic 'tsunami'
Both Kalshi and Polymarket were quick to celebrate big wins on midterm election night, touting what they say was accurate forecasting.

With billions waged on these prediction markets, which allowed traders to bet on candidate victories and control of the Senate and House, their accuracy was pushed into the spotlight. Media companies such as CNN and MSNBC shared prediction-market odds in their midterm coverage, while rappers such as YG and actors such as Heidi Montag weighed in on their midterm bets on election night.

According to Kalshi's midterm election recap, $2.5 billion US was traded on midterm markets, nearly double the $1.3 billion US reported during the 2024 election cycle. Polymarket recorded nearly $700 million US in wagers during this election cycle across its U.S. and international platforms, according to Reuters.
Polymarket said on X that the prediction-market platform was "right" and claimed that "98.4 per cent of resolved midterm races went to the Polymarket favorite the day before Election Day."
Kalshi made a similar claim, saying candidates favoured on its platform won or lead 98 per cent of races before polls closed on election day.
Valerie Cross, head of emerging verticals at NEXTPredict.io, which monitored Kalshi and Polymarket on election night, said that while those figures aren't necessarily wrong, "it's easy to overread."
She added that the figures reflect how prediction markets were able to incorporate "early returns, exit polls and county counts quickly, and mostly moved in the right direction."
"They were also early to flag upsets, because raw vote counts can make a race look closer than the odds imply," she said.
What happens when election betting goes mainstream
Predicting a blue tsunami
But while the platforms might have been mostly accurate about who would win, they didn't predict some of the most surprising races of the night.
An analysis by Betting Intelligence of more than 400 races identified 14 upsets, all won by Democrats.

One was the South Carolina Senate race, where prediction markets had favoured Republican candidate Darline Graham to win, giving her about a 70 per cent chance before Democrat Annie Andrews unexpectedly won.
Other upsets included Democrat Gina Hinojosa's victory over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas. Markets had put Hinojosa's chances at 40.1 per cent the day before the election.
The firm concluded that both polls and markets "identified the eventual winner equally often, and both underestimated Democratic candidates."

David Szakyoni, co-founder of the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, which analyzes prediction markets based on publicly available data, said the markets "appear to respond to the vote counts and polling data, rather than providing something distinct."
Rajiv Sethi, an economist at Columbia University, said neither polls nor prediction markets were able to "predict the scale" of Democratic wins on election night.
He instead pointed to races where both polls and markets were wrong as a way to better understand their effect, such as the extremely close Mississippi senate race.
(CBC)
The race has not yet been called by The Associated Press, with Democrat Scott Colom leading Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 1,803 votes as of Thursday afternoon.

Neither the polls nor the markets predicted the nail-biting margin between the two candidates, but Sethi said prediction markets gave Colom a slightly better chance than the polls suggested, pointing to their ability to react to candidate blunders or successes in the campaign.
"[Polls] can't pick up the really unusual novel things which markets can. That is the strength of market."
But even if markets can react more quickly they still rely on polling data as part of their forecasts.
"The markets respond to the models. If the models didn't exist, the markets would be pricing things quite differently."
Before the networks
Cross agreed that the markets can't always be pitted against polls.
"They measure different things at different times, and they depend on each other more than the headlines suggest."
She said, however, "For an early read on who's likely to win on Election Day, nothing really beats prediction markets."

"Traders are incorporating all the available information into their forecasts," Cross said. "At 8:12 p.m., with about 31 per cent counted in South Carolina, Andrews led 52 per cent to 46 per cent, and NBC said it was too early to call."
Polymarket CEO Shayne Copland said on X, "It's now routinely hours between when prediction markets call it versus the TV networks."
Prediction markets let you bet on anything — but is it just gambling?

Kalshi CEO Terek Mansour made a similar argument, saying, "For generations, election night meant turning on the TV and waiting for a handful of people to tell you what happened. Prediction markets change that."

According to Betting Intelligence, in most close races, prediction markets reached 97 per cent probability for the eventual winner about an hour before The Associated Press called the race. None of the candidates that reached that threshold lost.
Despite those early calls, Szakonyki said he's "not convinced that prediction markets added much value to the electoral conversation in this cycle."
Cross, however, said the volume of trading leaves little doubt about the level of interest.
"Midterms usually draw a fraction of the attention a presidential race gets. If a midterm can produce these numbers, 2028 could be several times larger."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ashley Fraser is the TikTok producer for CBC News and is currently a senior reporter for CBC's The National. Previously she worked as a field producer and audio producer at CBC Radio and CBC News. Her videos were part of the team that won a silver Digital Publishing Award in best news coverage for covering the 2024 U.S. election. Email her ashley.fraser@cbc.ca

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon tells double murder trial shooting of Jesse Baird wasn’t intentional but ‘it was my fault’
articles.summary: Former NSW police officer gives evidence for a second day after pleading not guilty to murdering Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon has said he is “guilty of manslaughter” but said shooting Jesse Baird wasn’t intentional, as he gave evidence in his double-murder trial.
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon continued giving evidence at the New South Wales supreme court on Friday. He described the moment he shot Baird, at which point Baird’s mother, Helen, left the courtroom.
“As police officers we are trained to shoot people at the centre of body mass … I had a split second moment where I said drop the knife … It was just police mode now,” he said from the witness box.
“If I didn’t do that I was 110% going to have that knife driven into my throat. And Jesse Baird was going to be sitting in my position today.”

blocks.caption: Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird (right). Composite: Supplied/NSW Supreme Court

blocks.text: He told the jury about an occasion when he went to the Royal national park with a friend and shot his gun. At this time he was thinking of taking his own life, and he wanted to test how loud his gun was, he told the jury.
He says he fired it at a tree. “I was very aware of making sure the bullet didn’t hit any innocent person,” Lamarre-Condon said.
The court also heard Lamarre-Condon signed out his firearm for a shift, three days before the alleged murders.
He had permission to do this, he told the court, and on the way to work had stopped at East Village shopping centre in Zetland to get his car washed.
The former officer claimed in court that it was common for police to get coffee or stop off elsewhere on the way to work.

He said he was thinking of stopping at Paddington to get his belongings from Baird before the other man got home from work, which would have put him in the “exact same” position he was in today as his firearm was still in his backpack.
On the day of the alleged murders, the officer said he wanted to retrieve his surfboard, clothes and Cartier ring from Baird’s home.
He took his mother’s car, because he did not want to be recognised, and began driving up and down Baird’s street to look for his ute, the jury heard.
Lamarre-Condon then parked the car in a spot left by Baird’s housemate, he told the jury.

He claimed he did not want to come into contact with Baird due to a risk the other man could take out an apprehended violence order against him as Baird had previously asked him to “please refrain from contacting me”.
Lamarre-Condon told the court he had seen what he assumed to be someone’s delivery motorcycle: “As soon as I saw that I had an idea … I saw a hi-vis hooded jacket, waterproof long pants and gloves.

“This moment here … I wish that I didn’t do this … But I had the thought process that if I was to put on this helmet and outfit I could knock on Jesse’s door I would look like an UberEats driver without any verbal interaction with Jesse,” he said.
The accused claimed Baird’s room was empty when he entered the home and that he looked through some storage boxes in the bedroom in search of his clothes but couldn’t find them.
Lamarre-Condon said he was still wearing the motorcycle helmet and his firearm in a holster under his shirt, when Baird saw him.
“He started yelling, ‘we’re getting robbed, we’re getting robbed’ … He couldn’t see it was me because the visor was down,” Lamarre-Condon said.
after newsletter promotion
At this point he claimed Baird lunged at him.
Lamarre-Condon claimed he aimed for Baird’s right shoulder and discharged the firearm.
The two continued to struggle but the officer’s finger remained on the trigger, the jury heard.

They tripped over a storage box on the ground, which is when Lamarre-Condon “accidentally” discharged the gun, he told the court: “It was my fault … I am guilty of manslaughter… But it wasn’t intentional.”
The jury heard he dialled the emergency hotline to try to get help for Baird.
But when he looked up, he saw Davies, who he didn’t recognise him at the time.
The accused claims the other man had picked up his gun.
“It was pointed towards me at my chest and he said ‘I’m going to fucking shoot you’,” he told the court.
“I started lowering my body towards the ground: I said, ‘Please don’t shoot me, I’m not here to shoot you. I’m not a threat I’m not here to hurt you.’
“That’s when he raised the gun towards my head and said, ‘Fuck off.”
The former officer said police are trained to redirect gun muzzles when firearms are pointed at them.
“I saw the gun, he was holding it with both hands I thought fuck he’s going to fire the gun and that’s where my police training kicked in,” he told the court.
“My left hand would have grabbed Luke’s left wrist and turned it away … my other hand pushed against the forearm and then I pushed the pivot point of the left wrist away from me.”
Asked by the defence lawyer whether the gun went off, Lamarre-Condon says:
“Yes, during this motion. And it got Luke.”
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Peru airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
articles.summary:
Three suitcases’ worth of the spiders were on their way to Germany, where they could fetch an estimated €1.5m

More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to…

blocks.text: More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.

The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.

They were spotted after agents noticed some unusual wriggling inside the luggage during a routine customs inspection at Jorge Chávez international airport. “We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones,” said Cora Suarez, a SERFOR wildlife control technician.

blocks.caption: The hatchlings were hidden inside a sock.   Photograph: SERFOR/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: One tarantula can sell for about €500 ($560) in Europe, Suarez said, meaning the wildlife trafficking scheme would be potentially worth €1.5m for just one trip.
The hidden arachnids, which came from several regions of Peru, were found in varying stages of development, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, Suarez said.
The Europeans accused of smuggling the tarantulas were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and will face criminal proceedings, SERFOR said.
Illegal wildlife trafficking is a highly lucrative criminal activity that generates around $20bn annually worldwide, according to Interpol.
Such trafficking is among the primary causes of the loss of biodiversity on the planet.

articles.title: Trump signs order preventing future presidents from changing Oval Office
articles.summary: The order comes after Trump made a series of big changes the Oval Office decor and launched landmark construction projects across Washington.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.
Trump, a former real estate mogul, has altered the president's official office during his second term, most notably by adding many gold features to its walls.

"So we're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.
American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.
Thursday's executive order declares the Oval Office to be a national monument, along with some of its surrounding rooms.

The document also says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".
"We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country," Trump said.

items: How Trump is remaking the White House in his own image

blocks.text: The president has the power to create national monuments, which are similar to national parks.
Trump's order calls on the office to be maintained by the National Park Service "in a manner that protects its historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency".
The entire building is already designated as a National Historic Landmark, which is intended to prevent against sudden changes to the building.

Trump's proclamation notes the existing protection, but says "nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance".

Congress has carved out an exemption to the National Historic Preservation Act, in order to allow presidents to make needed changes. The current Oval Office has existed since the early 1930s, after its conception by President Franklin D Roosevelt.

Greg Werkheiser, from the law firm Cultural Heritage Partners, which specialises in historic preservation, says that temporary alterations like "furniture and decor is completely up to the president's discretion".
"As long as they're not damaging the permanent art and architecture, they can generally do whatever they want," he tells BBC News.
Werkheiser argues that the Trump administration has shown extreme disregard for other historic sites in Washington, and through lawsuits has attempted to undermine the laws that require preservation.

Trump has undertaken a massive beautification project in Washington and has held three events in the past week to boast of the construction, even as his Republican party was trounced by Democrats in the midterm elections.

"The hypocrisy is that on the one hand he's talking about the importance of preserving the Oval Office - which is legally meaningless because he can't do it - and on the other hand he is absolutely taking an axe to the law that allows us to preserve other historic sites."

Werkheiser notes Trump's efforts to renovate the Kennedy Center in Washington DC, to build a new triumphal arch in the city, and to paint the granite exterior of the historic executive office building. His firm has filed lawsuits to block two of the projects.
In October, the president suggested in an interview with Time, external magazine that the Oval Office would need to be torn down due to security concerns from the US Secret Service.
"I said, 'My ass, you can't build a new one. This is a special place,'" Trump said at the time.

During the midterm election campaign Democrats criticised Trump's redesigns, with former President Barack Obama saying that his golden tweaks have "got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory".

articles.title: Trump declares his redesigned Oval Office a national monument
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday declaring the Oval Office and Cabinet room of the White House to be national monuments.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday declaring the Oval Office and the Cabinet room of the White House to be national monuments, which he said will prevent future administrations from making significant modifications. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
U.S. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday declaring the Oval Office and Cabinet room of the White House to be national monuments.
In week of midterm thumping, Trump holds 3rd event focused on a Washington renovation project
U.S. President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday declaring the Oval Office and Cabinet room of the White House to be preserved as national monuments.

Trump said his proclamation will prevent future presidents from making major changes to the two White House rooms — which he has extensively redecorated since the start of his second term — without the approval of Congress.

"It will make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space," he told reporters in the Oval Office. "It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people."

Even though the White House is designated a National Historic Landmark, Trump has demolished its East Wing to build a new ballroom, paved over the Rose Garden and built a concrete helipad on the South Lawn, all since his return to the presidency last year and without Congressional approval.

In a week when Trump's Republican Party suffered a dramatic smackdown in the midterm elections, this was the third day in which the president has made one of his Washington, D.C. renovation projects the central subject of his media event.
On Wednesday, he took the White House press pool to the ballroom site and put his signature on a concrete beam.
Trump has overseen a gold-tinged redecoration of the Oval Office interior. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)
On Monday, the final day of the midterm campaign, he gave a speech to mark the conclusion of the problem-plagued renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Trump's declaration of the Oval Office and Cabinet room as national monuments was his first official presidential action since the midterm loss.
'Of great interest to me'
He called the move "something that is of great interest to me, but it's of great interest to a lot of people."

As Trump signed the proclamation, a red baseball cap with "VETO" in white letters sat on his desk. The U.S. president has the power to veto legislation that falls short of a two-thirds majority in either the House or the Senate.

items: Trump 'out of touch with reality' about midterm losses, says Republican strategist
What the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada

blocks.text: Trump's focus on renovations is raising questions about his political priorities, particularly in light of the drubbing the Republicans took in the midterms.
His Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, only the third time that has happened to a sitting president's party during a midterm election in the past 80 years.
A view of the Oval Office on Jan. 20, 2021, the first day of then-president Joe Biden's term in office. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

The Democratic Party flipped seven GOP Senate seats, including from deep red states such as Texas, Kansas and Iowa. The Democrats won at least 253 Congressional districts, putting them on track for the biggest House margin that any party has held since 1990.
Key Republicans have been quick to point fingers over the midterm loss.

items: JD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?
Ohio and Texas went from red to blue in the midterms but may not stay that way in 2028

blocks.text: Texas Sen. Ted Cruz blamed the election loss on elected Republicans dismissing voters' concerns about the cost of living.
"Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long," Cruz said Wednesday on his podcast Verdict.
"Too many Republican politicians seem like they didn’t understand or they didn’t care,” he said.
Earlier Wednesday, U.S. Vice-President JD Vance blamed the results on the war in Iran, while Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Republican messaging didn't address the real concerns of voters.

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

articles.title: Trump signs proclamation to try to prevent changes to gold-covered Oval Office
articles.summary:
President seeks to make Oval Office a national monument to ensure designs are not ‘ripped down by stupid people’

Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he says will prevent…

blocks.text: Donald Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday that he says will prevent future administrations from changing his design of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, spaces which he declared as national monuments that should be preserved.

In the days since his party suffered historic defeats in the midterm elections, the president has seemingly turned his attention to the many renovation projects he has begun across the nation’s capital. Sitting behind the Resolute Desk on Thursday, Trump declared the Oval Office a “national monument”.
“I’m going to be signing a document which will make them into a landmark for the ages,” he told reporters in the gold-covered Oval Office.

According to the president, the proclamation would ensure the West Wing rooms would not be “touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape”.
“I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come and take it down and try and do something with it,” he said.

“Every once in a while they’ll look and they’ll say, oh, maybe what we’ll do is we’ll put some glass up that’s a little bit better or something, and I say no, you’re not going to do anything. We’re going to leave this as it is,” he continued.
“If anyone ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you’ll call me wherever I may be, and I will come back here and I will make sure it never happens.”

Since returning to office, Trump has embarked on a series of White House “beautification” projects, most notably the demolition of the East Wing to make way for a $600m ballroom, as well the building of a permanent granite helipad on the South Lawn.

Speaking to reporters from the Oval Office, the president defended his wider renovation work at the White House, saying the building’s exterior had suffered from years of deterioration. He pointed to cracked windows, damaged stonework and broken decorative features, saying he had paid for repairs and hired skilled workers to restore them.
“When you looked at that wall one year ago, it was badly damaged from years of service,” he said, adding that exterior columns had also been in “horrible shape”.

On the desk next to where he signed the proclamation was a red baseball cap emblazoned with the word “Veto” – an explicit reminder of his threat to block the legislative priorities and bills passed by the new Democratic-controlled Congress next year.

blocks.caption: The baseball hat with ‘Veto’ written on the front. Photograph: Shawn Thew-Pool/CNP/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Democrats made significant gains in several traditionally Republican states where Trump had previously won, including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa, by campaigning on issues including affordability and tackling corruption, while also securing control of Congress.

Trump’s opulent redesign of the Oval Office has drawn criticism, including from former president Barack Obama, who recently joked that “he’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere.”
Obama’s remark prompted a coordinated response from the White House, with treasury secretary Scott Bessent appearing to hit back by dining at a Cheesecake Factory.

In a final appeal ahead of the midterm elections, Trump held a press conference highlighting the delayed results of his $14m renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, while blaming Joe Biden for the algae that had accumulated in its waters.
“This was in the Biden era … Look, it’s not an easy thing. The algae is brutal. It forms easily. All you saw was dirt and filth and paper and everything else for years,” Trump said on Monday.
Two days later, as the scale of his party’s staggering losses came into focus, Trump led a media tour of the White House Ballroom construction site, where he marveled at the renovations to come.
“The whole thing is a miracle,” he said.

articles.title: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo, who had part of a lung removed last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

blocks.text: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
Image source, Reuters
Pope Leo is travelling to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
BySarah Rainsford
Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Rome

Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".

It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.

At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
Back on track

"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."

blocks.caption: Image caption, On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
On Friday Pope Leo presided over the annual memorial Mass for cardinals and bishops who have died
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced

blocks.text: Father Fernando Laguna said his heart was filled with joy when the Pope's visit to Argentina was announced
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.

"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"

The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.

blocks.caption: Image caption, 'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome

blocks.text: 'Welcome Pope Leo' reads this poster in the Argentinian church in Rome

This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
'Homecoming' to Peru
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025

blocks.text: Worshippers at Chiclayo cathedral in Peru were delighted when their former bishop became Pope in 2025
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title: Florida puts man to death as three US executions scheduled for same day
articles.summary:
Indiana executed a man hours earlier, and in Alabama, a man was scheduled to die by injection later

Florida carried out a record-tying 19th execution of the year on Thursday in an unusual…

blocks.text: Florida and Alabama plan to execute one man each on Thursday just hours after Indiana put a prisoner to death – in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for the same day in the US.

It would be Florida’s 19th execution this year under the Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, matching a record set by the state in 2025, and the second time this year that three people would be put to death on the same day.

The death penalty in the US has faced renewed scrutiny since the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions after she survived two massive doses of pentobarbital.
In Indiana on Thursday, Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, was pronounced dead at 12.45am at the state prison in Michigan City, said Noelle Russell, spokesperson at the state’s department of correction.

She said he had no final words. He had acknowledged killing his girlfriend’s two children in a house fire in the Evansville area in 2010 but had hoped that governor Mike Braun would grant clemency and change his sentence to life in prison. Braun declined.
Florida has carried out more than half the 32 executions in the US so far this year.

Jesse Guardado is set for execution later on Thursday after being convicted of fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton county home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. She had helped him get a job and housing. Guardado, now 64, had a court appeal turned down.

In Alabama, Michael Taylor is set to die by lethal injection on Thursday. In 1991, when he was 19, he beat two people, aged 83 and 79, to death with a metal bar during a robbery in their home in Gadsden.
Death penalty opponents had urged Alabama’s Republican governor, Kay Ivey, to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, but she declined.

Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty said: “If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life whom it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today.”

The state plans to execute Taylor, 54, by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.

Alabama executed murderer Kenneth Smith in 2024 by nitrogen asphyxiation, in an episode that witnesses found excruciating, after previously failing to succeed in its attempt to kill him using lethal injection.

Meanwhile, in Indiana earlier on Thursday, lawyers failed to persuade the state governor to allow Weisheit to undergo brain scans to assess a history of head injuries and mental health problems. They had asked for a life sentence.

Weisheit’s last objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week in front of the Indiana pharmacy board, the state regulatory agency.

The execution provided “long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty”, Indiana attorney general Todd Rokita said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Cavite pet crematorium contracted Bulacan couple to cremate pets — NBI
articles.summary: Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, contracted a married couple in San Jose del Monte City, Bulacan, to cremate dead pets entrusted to the establishment, the National Bureau of…

blocks.text: November 6, 2026 | 7:42am
A blurred image shows the remains of pets found inside plastic bags dumped along a roadside in San Jose del Monte City, Bulacan.
Luna and Furry Siblings via Facebook
Content warning: This article contains references to dumped animal remains.

MANILA, Philippines — Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, contracted a married couple in San Jose del Monte City, Bulacan, to cremate dead pets entrusted to the establishment, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said on Thursday, November 5.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag said the Bacoor-based crematorium had initially ordered cremation equipment, but the machinery was never delivered, forcing the establishment to outsource the service to the couple.
The couple was supposed to cremate the animals and return their ashes to Ahjay Paws for release to their respective owners.
However, the couple allegedly could not accommodate the volume of dead pets sent to their facility and resorted to burying some of the remains instead of cremating them.

“Ang findings na natin dito, Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium, wala siyang facility, wala siyang equipment to do the cremation. So pinadala niya doon. Malaki 'yung volume ng dumarating,” Matibag said in an interview with GMA News.
(Our findings here: Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium had no facility or equipment to perform cremations, so the animals were sent there. A large volume was being delivered.)
Matibag said the couple eventually buried the animals, while some remains were dumped instead of being properly disposed of.
“So ang ginawa nila, linibing nila,” he added, citing the couple's testimony.
(So what they did was bury them.)

The dead animals were transported from Bacoor to San Jose del Monte City using a delivery courier service. Matibag said the courier was unaware that the packages contained animal remains because these were placed in sacks and plastic bags.
The couple surrendered to the NBI on Wednesday, November 4, and submitted statements detailing how the animals were handled. They also expressed willingness to testify in the investigation.

“We will help the Department of Justice identify who qualifies as a witness to further establish who has liabilities, but there is already a sworn statement based on the investigation of the Environmental Crime Division,” Matibag explained.
The NBI will forward the complaints to the Department of Justice, which will determine whether the couple may qualify as state witnesses.

The investigation follows the discovery of the remains of 26 dogs and three cats in plastic bags along a roadside in San Jose del Monte City on October 31. Bacoor City Mayor Strike Revilla ordered the closure of Ahjay Paws and directed the police to investigate its owner.
Matibag said a total of 49 dead pets had been linked to the couple, including those recently found in Bulacan.

The NBI will initially file six cases based on the complaints submitted to the bureau, with Matibag saying investigators already have sufficient evidence to bring the matter before the prosecutor's office.
The agency is also investigating possible violations of sanitation and environmental laws arising from the transportation and disposal of the animal remains.
The crematorium's management could also face estafa and violations of the Consumer Protection Act.
Meanwhile, around 250 pet owners are expected to file complaints against Ahjay Paws, according to earlier statements from local authorities.
The NBI is also looking into the possible liability of other individuals involved in the operation and seeking an Immigration Lookout Bulletin Order to prevent them from leaving the country.

articles.title: Democratic socialist defeats incumbent Karen Bass in Los Angeles mayor's race
articles.summary: The results mean America's two most populous cities - New York and Los Angeles - will be led by democratic socialists.

blocks.text: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.

Raman's win stunned political watchers in California after she entered the race as a long-shot candidate against Bass, a political heavyweight who previously served in Congress and had never lost a race for political office.
Raman has frequently been compared to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are democratic socialists and ran on progressive platforms.

Her win solidifies that America's two biggest cities will now be led by democratic socialists, which include some of the most high-profile politicians in the US, such as Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
Los Angeles was always likely to have a Democratic mayor but the question in the city - the second most populous city in the US - was just how left voters would be willing to go.

Bass, also Democrat, announced that she had called and conceded to Raman in a post on social media on Thursday, writing "while this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken."

"Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote. "I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

items: Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch

blocks.text: Raman, a member of city council and Indian immigrant, ran on a platform of change and fixing the "broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again".

She ran on cutting homelessness, increasing housing in the city, saving Hollywood jobs from continued cuts and protecting residents from immigration enforcement efforts. Raman also vowed to fix the city's many issues, including helping beautification efforts, fixing roads and even helping bring back nightlife in the city.

The major issue in the race, however, was the LA fires, which killed dozens of people and razed neighbourhoods across the area in 2025. Bass faced intense political fallout over her absence during the emergency and the city's response to the disaster.
The next mayor in LA will oversee hosting the Super Bowl in 2027 and the 2028 Summer Olympics.

articles.title: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
articles.summary: The Delhi government has announced a four-month winter action plan, but experts say that won't be enough.

blocks.text: There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.

Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?

This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.

Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.

This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.

For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.

The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.

Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.

Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Expert say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.

"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.

"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."

Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.

"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."

Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.
This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.

items: 'I panic every time she coughs' - Delhi's toxic air is making its children sick
Why India caps pollution reading at 500 when the air is far more toxic
Can artificial rain fix toxic air in India's capital?
Living in Delhi smog is like watching a dystopian film again and again

blocks.text: In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.
During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".

On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.

The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".
Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.
A 2025 report, external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.
For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.

Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.
While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.
Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.
Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.
The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi.
"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.
"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

articles.title: PR expert says author Steven Galloway had path to rehabilitate reputation
articles.summary: Galloway, a former University of British Columbia writing professor, is suing multiple people who published allegations of sexual assault against him.

image.caption: Bestselling author Steven Galloway is seen in his former office at the University of British Columbia in March 2014. A public relations expert testified on Thursday in an ongoing defamation trial launched by Galloway. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Galloway, a former University of British Columbia writing professor, is suing multiple people who published allegations of sexual assault against him.
Author is suing his accuser and others over statements about him
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 05, 2026 6:10 PM EST | Last Updated: 6 minutes ago

A public relations expert told British Columbia Supreme Court that author and former University of B.C. professor Steven Galloway could have done more to rehabilitate his reputation after he was accused of rape more than a decade ago.

Norman Stowe, a reputation rehabilitation, public relations and crisis management expert, testified on Thursday in the trial of Galloway's defamation lawsuit against his accuser and others who published unproven allegations against him.

"To be blunt, I've worked with clients who had far less going for them than Mr. Galloway in terms of the capacity to go out and defend your reputation or rehabilitate your reputation," said Stowe, a managing partner of the public affairs company Pace Group.

Stowe produced a report for the defence of Galloway's accuser, a woman known as A.B., whose name is subject to a publication ban. He told the court that while he had never worked on a file involving a rape accusation, efforts to rehabilitate someone's reputation involve the same steps regardless of the nature of the issue.
Former UBC professor Steven Galloway’s defamation trial begins

The trial heard Stowe's report included examples of other high-profile people who suffered reputational damage, such as Bill Clinton, Martha Stewart and Tiger Woods, but he agreed under cross-examination that allegations against them were not in the same "universe" as a rape accusation.
A.B.'s defence does not allege she was sexually assaulted, rather that she reported the alleged assaults.
Galloway denies the assault claims, and alleges they destroyed his career.

items: Steven Galloway testifies that faculty-student relationships in UBC arts program were common
'Outrageous' rhetoric alleged in emails as Steven Galloway defamation trial continues

blocks.text: The court previously heard from a publishing industry expert who said the author of the hit novel The Cellist of Sarajevo had potentially lost millions of dollars in future income.

Stowe said some of Pace Group's high-profile clients have included the Vancouver Airport Authority following the death of Robert Dziekanski — who died after being Tasered by Mounties at the airport in 2007 — and B.C. Ferries after the sinking of the Queen of the North.
"We have also worked on several cases that involve sexual activities. I can't say much more than that," he said.
Multiple people apologized
The court heard Stowe believed Galloway had a "strong path to reputational rehabilitation" and could have resumed some version of his writing career.
But he conceded under questioning by Galloway's lawyer, Daniel Burnett, that his report incorrectly stated the author had made no efforts to do so.
Burnett said Stewart, Clinton and Woods were all "guilty" of what they'd been accused of, and asked Stowe about a different approach to restoring the reputation of someone who is innocent.

Stowe said he didn't have access to some documents in Galloway's case, including the full report by a retired judge, Mary Ellen Boyd, who found the assault allegations against the author unsubstantiated.

Stowe told the court Boyd's report could have been used as leverage in rehabilitating Galloway's reputation, along with support from those in the literary community who had publicly called for due process for the author.
Bestselling author Steven Galloway's defamation trial in 4th week
But Stowe said "there was no plan, no linking these things together to help him get past this and rehabilitate so he could reclaim some part of his personal life and professional life."
Stowe believed Galloway had many opportunities "to bring all these things together, but that never seemed to materialize," he said.
He said he thought the author had "sort of given up," thinking "his life was over."

He agreed that rape allegations are "powerful." But he said Galloway's attempts to refute the claims against him were not part of a plan to rehabilitate his reputation, and the efforts "sort of started and then stalled."

items: UBC prof testifies she acted as a 'conduit' for sex assault allegations against Steven Galloway
Sex assault allegations diminished performance of Steven Galloway's books: industry expert

blocks.text: Stowe said he didn't review social media posts about Galloway, which Burnett said came in "waves … over years and years" leading to the defamation lawsuit.
Stowe's testimony concluded Thursday and defendant Mandi Gray was next to take the stand.
Galloway alleges Gray, an assistant professor at Trent University in Ontario, defamed him in a series of social media posts.
Several people originally named as defendants in Galloway's lawsuit, filed in 2018, have settled with him and offered public apologies.

image.caption: Branko Bijelic appears by video link in B.C. Provincial Court in Vancouver on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (CBC News)

blocks.text: British Columbia
One of two people charged in relation to the death of an 11-year-old Burnaby boy appeared in a Vancouver courtroom for the first time on Thursday.
Branko Bijelic is charged with 2nd-degree murder in the death of Kai Pavlovic
One of two people charged in relation to the death of an 11-year-old Burnaby, B.C., boy appeared in a Vancouver courtroom for the first time on Thursday.
Branko Bijelic, 51, is charged with second-degree murder and indignity to human remains in the death of Kai Pavlovic.
He and 46-year-old Sarah Bijelic, who was also charged with manslaughter in the case, were both family members of the boy, according to police.
A publication ban prevents CBC News from reporting on any details about Sarah Bijelic's court proceedings.
Police allege Kai Pavlovic was killed prior to being reported missing on Sept. 26, 2025. (Submitted by Burnaby RCMP)
Branko, who has yet to enter a plea, appeared by video link dressed in a red sweatshirt and glasses.
He sat quietly during proceedings, which were put over until later this month.

items: Family members charged in homicide of missing 11-year-old Burnaby, B.C., boy

blocks.text: A family member from New Zealand, who identified herself as Kai's grandmother, was present in court gallery, but declined to speak with journalists.
In a statement to CBC News, Kai's aunt Helen Kok said the family remains "absolutely devastated" by his death, and will "forever have a Kai shaped hole in our hearts."
Kai's aunt Helen Kok said the family remains 'absolutely devastated' by his death, and will 'forever have a Kai shaped hole in our hearts.' (Submitted by Burnaby RCMP)
"Kai was the light of our lives and we will miss the joy, creativity, and sense of adventure he brought with him wherever he went — and that is how we will remember him," the statement adds.
"We are grateful for closure after a long time of not knowing."
The family also asked the public to refrain from judgement, conjecture and speculation.

The boy's remains were discovered at an undisclosed location earlier this year, according to IHIT. (Submitted by Burnaby RCMP)
According to police, Burnaby RCMP had received a request to check on the boy's well-being that day, and escalated the case to the Serious Crimes Unit when they were unable to locate him.
The case was later escalated again to IHIT.

Family members have launched a fundraiser with the goal of transporting Kai's remains to Montenegro so he can be buried with his father, and for the creation of a memorial garden in New Zealand.

articles.title: L.A. has a new mayor, and she's a democratic socialist
articles.summary: Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation's…

image.caption: Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, will be the next mayor of Los Angeles after defeating incumbent Mayor Karen Bass. (Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

Nithya Raman, a little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, has defeated Mayor Karen Bass, an upset that will alter the trajectory of the nation's second-largest city.
Nithya Raman makes L.A. the 4th U.S. city to elect democratic socialist to top job

The India-born Raman's upstart campaign marked a generational shift at city hall as voters followed the lead of New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected last year. Raman, though, never attracted the same level of national attention and stressed her willingness to break with the progressive party at times during the campaign.

When she takes office next month, Raman, 45, will join the vanguard of democratic socialists in municipal government. In addition to Mamdani, Janeese Lewis George was elected Tuesday as mayor of Washington, D.C., and Katie Wilson is mayor in Seattle.
Asked about the success of democratic socialists in mayoral contests, U.S. President Donald Trump said "we'll see what happens" but warned the impact of the changes they make might be irreversible.

"There'll be a point at which if people are unhappy, they'll be changed," Trump said in the Oval Office. "But unfortunately, usually that happens so late that you'll never be able to bring back a city or a country or a state. You know — when it goes too far."

Raman's entry into the race marked a stunning change of heart after she had initially endorsed Bass, 73, who was once her ally. She said the city had reached a "breaking point" and announced her own candidacy just before the filing deadline.
Bass calls to congratulate victor
Bass said in a statement that she called Raman to congratulate her on her victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," Bass said. "I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us."
Incumbent mayoral candidate Karen Bass, seen at a news conference in L.A. last week, was defeated in the election. (Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press)

Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a bid for re-election. Her first term was undone by the deadly Palisades fire, which ignited when she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. The devastation left many voters with the unshakeable feeling that Bass should be held to account, and she never recovered.

As votes were being counted earlier this week, Raman delivered an election night speech Tuesday that marked a campaign coda, summing up voters' frustration with a city that seemed to be adrift, and her vision for the future.

"For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do," she said. "L.A. stopped being a place where we could build things, where we could open things, where we could film things, where we could create things."
She said she would restore "that ambitious Los Angeles, that joyful Los Angeles, that creative Los Angeles, that entrepreneurial Los Angeles."
Raman's rise came in a year that saw Democratic divisions across the country, with insurgent left-wing candidates challenging establishment rivals.
Raman wants police chief ousted
Raman is promising to oust the police chief, whom she views as too accommodating with federal immigration authorities.
She also wants to improve basic services that have deteriorated for years, leaving neighbourhoods with dirty, pothole-ridden streets, buckled sidewalks and broken streetlights.
Ballots are inspected on election day Tuesday. (William Liang/The Associated Press)

Raman called Bass's efforts to reduce homelessness ineffective. She's promising a new approach on the crisis that would expand medical teams for people who live in encampments and on the streets in an effort to build trust and eventually bring them indoors.
Raman also wants to provide more housing to move people out of hotels rented by the city for those who are homeless.

She said her plans could reduce the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when the city will host the Olympic Games. However, the problem has long proved intractable, despite billions spent in the region.
Raman offered change
Raman was the face of change in a year when voters were restless over long-running problems that persisted under Bass.

A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted from Oct. 19 to 25 found that about four in 10 likely voters said reducing the number of homeless encampments should be a top priority for the next mayor to address, while about three in 10 said that about ensuring public safety or building more affordable housing.

items: Reality star Spencer Pratt out of L.A. mayor's race as progressive Nithya Raman advances

blocks.text: She was able to overcome criticism from Bass that she was "not ready for primetime" and too inexperienced to run a city with 3.8 million people, and she capitalized on anxiety over the future.

"Our city is in crisis," she said in one ad. The ad showed a lectern with no one behind it at the site of a massive warehouse fire from last summer, the homeless epicentre of Skid Row and shuttered malls and storefronts. "Where is our mayor?" Raman asked.
Bass argued that she made enough progress to merit a second four-year term, and she branded Raman's views on policing and homelessness as "extreme."
Top Democrats backed Bass

Raman's victory came despite limited backing from the Democratic establishment. Bass had support from California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former U.S. vice president Kamala Harris and former U.S. House speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with nearly every member of the city council.
Bass served in the state legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022 and was under consideration to be former U.S. president Joe Biden's running mate in 2020.

items: How AI has helped a former reality TV star become a contender for L.A. mayor

blocks.text: In an important signal to the business community, billionaire developer Rick Caruso said he was voting for Bass, but stopped short of formally endorsing the candidate he lost to in the 2022 mayoral race.

Raman, an urban planner, picked up notable support from advocacy and political groups, including Our Revolution, which was founded by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. But she was thin on endorsements from prominent local politicians.
She landed a widely publicized private meeting with former governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, who was not involved in the race, that hinted at her efforts to broaden her circle.

Expanding her network of allies could be crucial as she begins governing a city that's home to a struggling entertainment industry, a major port, world-class universities and research institutions, and serves as a major tourist destination.

articles.title: Fox News suffers ratings slump on bleak election night for Republicans
articles.summary: In early, preliminary figures, the news channel trailed several other networks in prime-time viewership

blocks.text: On a midterm election night that was a huge disappointment for Republicans, with Democrats taking control of the US House and Senate, the country’s most prominent conservative television network seemingly felt the brunt of viewer disillusionment with Donald Trump and his party, according to final audience numbers released on Thursday.

The Fox News Channel, which often leads among all news networks in viewership on election nights, fell behind two top broadcasters on Tuesday. According to ratings dating from the Nielsen firm, the network averaged 4.3 million total viewers between 8 and 11pm, behind broadcast networks NBC (6.7 million viewers) and ABC (5.2 million viewers), though it edged out fellow cable networks CNN (4.1 million viewers) and MS Now (3.7 million viewers). Fox News handedly defeat CBS News, which attracted just 2.8 million viewers. CNN performed better in the 25-to-54 age demographic prized by advertisers, besting Fox News, MS Now and CBS.
Originally, preliminary viewership numbers released Wednesday put Fox News behind both CNN and MS Now in total viewership in primetime.

Overall, the big six television networks averaged nearly 27 million total viewers during prime-time election coverage, up from 22.215 million total viewers in 2022. During those 2022 elections, Fox News averaged 7.422 million viewers, meaning its viewership slipped about 41% on Tuesday.

With Trump reaching historic levels of unpopularity, Fox News has seen some viewers tune out in recent weeks. Last month, the network’s viewership was down 27% compared with the same month last year in total day viewers, though it still handily defeated CNN and MS Now. Lachlan Murdoch, the chief executive of parent company Fox Corp, acknowledged “viewer fatigue” in an earnings call on Monday.

Trump, who criticized Fox throughout election night and blamed the network for his party’s losses, poked fun at the network’s October figures in a Truth Social post, chalking up the decline to the channel’s industry-standard practice of booking Democratic candidates for interviews.

“FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” he wrote on Tuesday evening. “All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me – My numbers are better than they have ever been.”
This story was updated on Thursday afternoon to reflect final viewership figures released by Nielsen.

articles.title: Will Atiku Abubakar be on Nigeria's presidential ballot after court ruling?
articles.summary: The high court has sacked the leadership of the opposition ADC party with only months to go until elections.

blocks.text: Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).
Among them were Abubakar - who had served as vice-president between 1999 and 2007 when the PDP was in power - and former Senate president David Mark.
As accommodations were made for the line-up of political heavyweights, Mark took over as its interim chairman.
But Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued before the court that this was not lawful as Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention.
Instead, he said, he himself should have taken over the party's leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025.
This is not first time the Federal High Court in the capital, Abuja, has ruled on the leadership of the party.
In July, judge Musa Liman said Mark had been chosen in accordance with the country's laws and the party's constitution - in a case brought by another former ADC member.
Abubakar said the latest case raised serious legal concerns: "Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute?"

In a statement, the ADC added that Thursday's judgement by Justice Peter Lifu was aimed at stifling the opposition momentum and "was a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy.
The ADC is seen as the most powerful opposition to President Tinubu. Many influential politicians opposed to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) have already defected to the party.
The legal saga could complicate things - it may cause uncertainty for hundreds of ADC candidates as well as raise questions over who has the authority to represent them.
But Abubakar, who is running for the presidency for a seventh time, is confident the matter will be resolved and called on his supporters not to be distracted.

"Nigerians deserve relief from this crushing cost-of-living crisis. We urge our supporters to remain resolute, take our message from house to house and door to door, and stay peaceful and focused," the 79-year-old said.
Peter Obi - the other main presidential candidate, who is on the ballot for a second time - has said he is shocked by Thursday's high court ruling.
He released a statement on X with the heading, external: "Do not undermine democracy".
The 65-year-old went on to say: "My concern is that three months before a general election, it is in the public interest to have certainty.
Obi had briefly joined the ADC before leaving earlier this year to join the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) - in part because of the legal challenges within the ADC.

"The sustenance of democracy in Nigeria, in the midst of encroaching military rule in West Africa, should strengthen our resolve to protect opposition politics and not stamp out opposition parties," he said.
The NDC's candidate said that, as president, he would ensure that the existence of opposition parties would be respected.
"This is a time to strengthen our democracy by allowing the opposition to thrive."
Additional reporting by Chris Ewokor in Abuja
